content: This protocol serves as a standardized framework for reviewing pain management strategies during labor, ensuring consistency in methodology and outcome collection across studies. Unlike typical Cochrane protocols that evolve into full reviews, this protocol will remain as a permanent reference to guide the development of all reviews on labor pain management. Each individual review will include specific background information about the intervention being studied, in addition to the general context provided by this protocol. Labor pain is influenced by a complex interplay of physiological and psychosocial factors. The intensity of pain experienced during labor varies widely among women. In rare cases, some women report no pain and deliver unexpectedly, while others describe labor pain as the most severe pain they have ever experienced. Pain during labor originates from different anatomical sites depending on the stage of labor. In the first stage of labor, which spans from the onset of labor to full cervical dilation, pain is primarily visceral and cramp-like. It arises from uterine contractions and cervical dilation, with pain signals transmitted via spinal nerves T10 to L1. This pain may radiate to the abdominal wall, lower back, iliac crests, gluteal regions, and thighs. The transition phase, occurring between 7 cm and 10 cm of cervical dilation, marks the shift to the second stage of labor. The second stage of labor, from full cervical dilation to the delivery of the baby, is characterized by pain from the distension of the vagina, perineum, and pelvic floor. Pain in this stage is transmitted via the pudendal nerves, which enter the spinal cord through nerve roots S2 to S4. This stage involves both visceral pain from uterine contractions and cervical stretching, as well as somatic pain from the stretching of vaginal and perineal tissues. Women also experience rectal pressure and a strong urge to push as the baby descends into the pelvic outlet. Several factors influence the perception and intensity of labor pain, including parity and the management of labor. Nulliparous women (those giving birth for the first time) generally report higher levels of sensory pain during early labor compared to multiparous women. The positions women adopt and their mobility during labor can also significantly affect pain perception. For example, upright or lateral positions during the second stage of labor are associated with reduced reports of severe pain compared to lying on the back. Induced labor is often perceived as more painful than spontaneous labor. Psychosocial factors also play a critical role in shaping the experience of labor pain. These include prior experiences with childbirth, cultural and ethnic background, educational level, and individual coping mechanisms. Historically, philosophies of pain control have evolved to address the fear-tension-pain cycle, a concept introduced by Grantly Dick-Read. He proposed that fear and anxiety lead to muscle tension, which amplifies the perception of pain. Strategies to break this cycle include education, relaxation techniques, and focused breathing. A variety of mind-body interventions are employed during pregnancy to reduce anxiety and prepare for labor. These include autogenic training, biofeedback, hypnosis, imagery, meditation, prayer, relaxation therapy, tai chi, and yoga. The physical and cultural environment of childbirth, as well as the emotional support provided by caregivers and birth companions, also significantly influence pain perception. Childbirth educators, midwives, and doulas use diverse approaches to prepare women for labor and manage pain. Two paradigms have been proposed to conceptualize these approaches: the pain relief paradigm and the working with pain paradigm. The pain relief paradigm views labor pain as unnecessary and advocates for the use of pain relief methods without guilt. In contrast, the working with pain paradigm emphasizes the physiological importance of pain in normal labor and supports the idea that women, with optimal support, can manage pain using their body's natural endorphins. Midwives play a crucial role in facilitating endorphin release by minimizing sensory stimulation. Research has shown that multi-dimensional interventions, such as continuous support, a supportive environment, and midwife-led care, can positively impact the perception of pain during childbirth. Continuous intrapartum support has been associated with shorter labor, higher rates of spontaneous vaginal birth, reduced use of analgesia, and greater satisfaction with the childbirth experience. Midwife-led continuity of care, involving a small team of midwives, has been linked to reduced use of pharmacological pain relief, fewer interventions, and an increased sense of control. A wide range of pain management methods is available to women during labor. Non-pharmacological interventions include hypnosis, biofeedback, sterile water injections, water immersion, aromatherapy, relaxation techniques (such as yoga, music, and guided audio), acupuncture, acupressure, massage, reflexology, and transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS). Pharmacological options include inhaled analgesia, opioids, non-opioid drugs, local anesthetic nerve blocks, and epidural or intrathecal injections of local anesthetics or opioids. Non-pharmacological methods primarily aim to help women cope with pain, while pharmacological methods focus on pain relief. Some interventions, such as hypnosis and relaxation techniques, are taught during antenatal classes and used before labor begins, while others, like epidurals and water immersion, are administered during labor. The development of this generic protocol for pain management in labor was funded by the National Institute for Health Research (NIHR) Cochrane-NHS Engagement Scheme. It aims to provide a comprehensive overview of evidence from individual reviews, making it easier for readers to access and understand the totality of evidence on this topic. The protocol was developed through active consultation with stakeholders, including members of the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group (PCG), review authors, consumers, and other experts. A core set of outcomes was identified and prioritized through collaboration with these stakeholders, ensuring that the protocol addresses the most important aspects of labor pain management.
